[1, 5, 8] The Crop Production report forecasted that American soft red winter (SRW) wheat production would reach 406 million bushels. [1] This figure represents a significant 21% increase from the production levels of 2022. [1] <3> A U.S. Wheat Associates report from April 25, 2023, highlighted the severe impact of a two-year drought on the hard red winter (HRW) wheat crop in the Central and Southern Plains. The report confirmed that the winter wheat condition was the lowest for that time of year since 1989, with just 26% of the crop rated as good to excellent. <4> Concerns over an extension of the Black Sea Grain Initiative, set to expire in mid-May 2023, created price volatility.; Russia had indicated it might not renew the deal, which allows for the safe export of Ukrainian grain, unless obstacles to its own grain and fertilizer exports were removed.; The deal allows for the safe export of Ukrainian grain. <5> The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) released its Prospective Plantings report on March 31, 2023, with data based on surveys of farm operators conducted in the first two weeks of March. The report estimated the total U.S. all-wheat planted area for 2023 at 49.9 million acres, marking a 9% increase from the previous year. This rise was primarily driven by winter wheat, with its planted area increasing by 13% to 37.5 million acres. In contrast, the area for spring wheat was projected to decrease by 2% to 10.6 million acres. <6> Following talks with the United Nations in Geneva, Russia proposed renewing the Black Sea Grain Initiative for 60 days, a significant reduction from the previous 120-day extensions. This proposal, made around March 13, 2023, immediately created market uncertainty ahead of the March 18 renewal deadline. Ukraine criticized the shorter term, stating it contradicted the original agreement which stipulated renewals of at least 120 days. The prospect of a shorter duration raised concerns about potential logistical problems and a slowdown in grain and oilseed shipments from Ukraine, as companies would be hesitant to risk their shipments getting stuck if the deal collapsed. This uncertainty had a direct impact on global food supply and U.S. wheat prices. <7> The USDA's monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, released on March 8, 2023, indicated no changes to the supply and demand outlook for U.S. wheat for the 2022/23 season compared to the previous month. [1, 2] While the U.S. outlook was stable, the global wheat forecast for 2022/23 anticipated slightly smaller supplies, increased consumption and trade, and lower ending stocks. [2] This uncertainty contributed to volatility in global wheat markets, with the UN's World Food Programme warning of catastrophic consequences for nations on the brink of famine if the deal was not extended. [2] Following talks in Geneva, the deal was officially extended on March 18, 2023, but only for 60 days rather than the previous 120, reflecting Russia's ongoing objections. [7] This downward pressure was primarily driven by a consistent supply of low-priced wheat from the Black Sea region. [7] Notably, Russia harvested a record wheat crop in the 2022/2023 marketing year, which significantly increased its export capacity and contributed to the ample global supply. [1, 2] This competitive pressure from both Russian and Ukrainian exports weighed on U.S. wheat futures, overriding domestic concerns about drought. [3] This represented the largest seeded area for winter wheat since the 2015/2016 season. [9] The increase was observed across various classes of wheat, with Hard Red Winter wheat area estimated at 25.3 million acres (a 10% increase), Soft Red Winter at 7.90 million acres (a 20% increase), and White Winter at 3.73 million acres (a 3% increase). Significant delays were attributed to heavy rains around the Fourth of July, which subsequently caused a drop in test weights for the last part of the crop, down to 56-57 pounds per bushel. [4, 9] The difficulties began with a prolonged drought, which was abruptly broken in mid-May by a weather pattern shift that brought repeated, heavy rainstorms. [4] This shift, while replenishing soil moisture, came at the wrong time for the wheat crop, idling combines for weeks and pushing the harvest into late July and even early August for some—a significant delay from the typical mid-June start. [4, 7] As of July 16, the harvest was only 71% complete, compared to the five-year average of 94%. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> China made significant purchases of U.S. Soft Red Winter (SRW) wheat in early December 2023; totaling over 1 million metric tons; These transactions were the largest of their kind to China in several years <2> The USDA's September Wheat Outlook, which was informed by the September 12, 2023, World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, held the forecast for all-wheat exports at 700 million bushels. Concurrently, the outlook revised the forecast for Hard Red Winter (HRW) wheat exports downward by 10 million bushels to 155 million. This projection for HRW exports marks the lowest level since record-keeping began in the 1973/74 marketing year. The reduction is attributed to the uncompetitiveness of U.S. HRW on the global market, which has been exacerbated by consecutive years of drought impacting supplies. <3> For the second consecutive year, and the third in a row, low water levels on the Mississippi River in the fall of 2023 created significant challenges for the transportation of grain. Hot and dry conditions led to historically low water levels, with some areas reporting lower levels than the same period in the previous year. This situation, occurring during the crucial harvest and export season, prompted restrictions on barge capacity to ensure navigability. Consequently, with more barges needed to transport the same amount of grain, barge freight rates surged. For instance, spot rates in St. Louis saw a 49% increase in a single week in late August 2023. This surge in transportation costs placed considerable financial pressure on farmers, often manifesting as a wider basis, which is the difference between the futures price and the local cash price they receive. While the market was reportedly better prepared for these conditions compared to the previous year, the increased costs still negatively impacted farmers' profitability. <4> In the summer of 2023, field crop news reports highlighted significant concerns over the quality of the winter wheat harvest due to persistent rainfall and poor weather, which delayed harvesting in some regions. The wet conditions increased the risk of pre-harvest sprouting, a cause of low falling numbers, which can lead to the grain being downgraded from milling quality to feed. Reports also noted the prevalence of Black Point, a fungal discoloration on kernels that can result in brown-to-black specks in flour, potentially causing rejection. Subsequent analysis in October 2023 confirmed lower quality for the harvest, with the average Hagberg Falling Number (HFN) at its lowest since 2017 and reduced specific weights, impacting flour milling extraction rates. <5> A market report in mid-August 2023 claimed an optimistic trend for U.S. wheat prices, citing increased global demand and reduced domestic yields. While persistent and severe drought conditions in the Great Plains did significantly reduce domestic wheat yields for the 2023/24 crop, with some analyses comparing the impact to the Dust Bowl years [5, 8], the claim of a broad optimistic trend driven by strong global demand is contradicted by more authoritative sources. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Economic Research Service, in its August 15, 2023 report, projected that U.S. all-wheat exports would be at a 52-year low. [4, 7] The report specifically noted that Hard Red Winter (HRW) wheat exports were uncompetitive on the global market due to large, lower-priced supplies from Russia and the European Union. [4, 7] While some analysis pointed to rising prices from global inquiries [1], other market indicators showed Chicago wheat futures falling to a three-week low early in the month. [2] Therefore, the market condition was more complex than a simple optimistic trend, with the significant reduction in domestic supply being offset by weak international demand for U.S. exports. <6> Throughout the second quarter of 2023, CBOT wheat futures experienced an 8.09% decline; contributing to a nearly 20% drop in the first half of the year.; The settlement price on June 30 was $6.3625 per bushel. <7> The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) announced that its global food price index averaged 123.9 points in July 2023, a 1.3% increase from the previous month. This rise was partly influenced by Russia's termination of the Black Sea Grain Initiative on July 17, 2023, which created uncertainty regarding Ukrainian exports. Specifically, the FAO Cereal Price Index recorded a 1.6% increase in wheat prices, marking the first monthly rise in nine months. In addition to the grain deal's termination, continued dry conditions in North America were also cited as a key driver for the increase in wheat prices. <8> The Kansas wheat harvest concluded by the end of July 2023, capping off one of the longest harvest seasons on record which extended for nearly two months for some farmers. Significant delays were attributed to heavy rains around the Fourth of July, which subsequently caused a drop in test weights for the last part of the crop, down to 56-57 pounds per bushel. Due to prior drought conditions, the state's overall wheat production for 2023 was projected to be the smallest since 1966, totaling an estimated 208 million bushels. <9> The 2023 Kansas winter wheat harvest was significantly delayed and challenging, marking one of the smallest crops since the 1960s. [4, 9] The difficulties began with a prolonged drought, which was abruptly broken in mid-May by a weather pattern shift that brought repeated, heavy rainstorms. [4] This shift, while replenishing soil moisture, came at the wrong time for the wheat crop, idling combines for weeks and pushing the harvest into late July and even early August for some—a significant delay from the typical mid-June start. [4, 7] As of July 16, the harvest was only 71% complete, compared to the five-year average of 94%. [4] The persistent moisture led to numerous complications, including a notable increase in weed pressure through the already thin wheat stands and the growth of secondary tillers, which complicated the dry-down process. [4] While early harvest reports showed good protein levels and test weights around 60 pounds per bushel, the ongoing rain delays caused a decline in test weights in later-harvested fields, dropping to 58 pounds or lower. [4, 7]

[1, 2, 3] The confluence of these events led to a short squeeze, catching traders by surprise and contributing to a 26% price rally over five weeks starting in late April. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The USDA's August 2025 Wheat Outlook, detailed in the World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, projected the 2025/26 season-average farm price for wheat at $5.30 per bushel. This represents a decrease of $0.10 per bushel. The price reduction was primarily attributed to anticipated pressure from lower U.S. corn prices. While domestic wheat production was revised downward, the export forecast was raised by 25 million bushels to 875 million, largely due to strong performance in Hard Red Winter Wheat. This increase in exports led to a reduction in projected ending stocks by 21 million bushels to 869 million. <2> A daily market wire on July 29, 2025, reported mixed results for U.S. wheat futures; CBOT September finishing unchanged at $5.38¾/bu; Kansas and Minneapolis contracts eased slightly <3> U.S. Wheat Associates published a price report.; The report provides representative price quotes.; The report provides price quotes for various classes of U.S. wheat. <4> A market report on July 24, 2025, confirmed that U.S. wheat markets were turning up, even amidst a generally bearish sentiment driven by favorable U.S. crop weather and solid harvest progress. Specifically, September CBOT wheat closed up by a penny at $5.41½ per bushel, September KC wheat increased by 5¢ to $5.28½, and September Minneapolis spring wheat rose by 2½¢ to $5.85½. Contributing to the upward movement, the USDA announced that weekly wheat export sales for the week ending July 17, 2025, were a higher-than-expected 712,200 tonnes (26.2 million bushels), easily surpassing trade expectations which ranged from 9 to 18.5 million bushels. <5> A global wheat market analysis for the second half of 2025 indicated a bearish sentiment for U.S. wheat futures; prices falling between 3.9% and 8.7% in the last week of June; influenced by expectations of a large EU harvest <6> On June 30, 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) released its quarterly Grain Stocks report, indicating that old crop U.S. wheat inventories as of June 1, 2025, were 851 million bushels (approximately 23.15 million metric tons). This represented a 22% increase from the previous year and was the highest stock level since 2018. The larger-than-anticipated surplus, which was slightly above market expectations, exerted downward pressure on wheat prices following the announcement. <7> In late June 2025, excessive rainfall and severe weather significantly delayed the winter wheat harvest in Kansas and Oklahoma. According to a USDA report for the week ending June 15, harvest progress was considerably behind the five-year average, with Kansas at 3% complete versus an 11% average, and Oklahoma at 30% complete compared to a 46% average. Persistent rain and high humidity kept combines out of fields, which in many areas were too wet to enter. These delays raised concerns about potential damage to crop quality, contributing to lower wheat condition ratings and worries about lower test weights and pre-harvest sprouting. <8> On June 10, 2025, wheat futures experienced a significant decline across all major U.S. contracts. Specifically, the Chicago, Minneapolis, and Kansas City contracts all reported losses exceeding 11 cents per bushel. This downturn was attributed to two primary factors: the agricultural consultancy SovEcon raising its 2025 wheat production forecast for Russia by 1.8 million tonnes to a total of 82.8 million tonnes, and an improved weather outlook that promised better chances of rain in key North American spring wheat regions. <9> New crop wheat sales for the 2025/26 U.S. marketing year surged due to a combination of competitive pricing, a weaker U.S. dollar, a more relaxed balance sheet, and timely moisture in growing areas. Between April 17 and May 22, 2025, sales increased by 170%. This growth shifted the sales pace from being 18% below the previous year to 60% ahead of the 2024/25 pace as of May 22. Significant year-over-year purchase increases were noted from key importers, including Mexico, the Philippines, and Japan. <10> On Monday, June 2, 2025, Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) July soft red winter wheat futures rose, settling up 5 cents at $5.39 per bushel. [3] The increase was attributed to several factors, including rising tensions in the Black Sea region, a weaker U.S. dollar, and some uncertainty about global production prospects. [3] According to traders cited by Reuters, these conditions prompted speculative short-covering. [3]
